blocks.text: 1. overview

blocks.alt: Actual positives feed recall, showing how many were found
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731268-761996873.png

Precision, the previous topic, measured how trustworthy a model's positive predictions actually were, of everything the model called positive, what fraction genuinely was. Recall measures the exact complementary question, looking at the same underlying confusion matrix categories from the opposite direction: of every genuine positive case that actually existed in the data, how many did the model actually manage to catch?

Recall goes by a couple of other names depending on the field or context it is being discussed in, most commonly Sensitivity in medical and clinical testing contexts, and True Positive Rate specifically within the ROC Curve topic covered later in this module, but all three names refer to the exact same underlying calculation, covered in full in this topic.
2. The Formula

blocks.alt: True positives divided by true positives plus false negatives gives recall
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731754-413497521.png

Recall is computed as True Positives divided by the sum of True Positives and False Negatives, using the same four confusion matrix categories already covered in the Accuracy and Precision topics. The denominator here, True Positives plus False Negatives, represents every single example that was actually, genuinely positive in the true labels, regardless of whether the model correctly identified it or missed it entirely.

This formula directly answers a precise, practical question: among every genuine positive case that actually existed in the evaluation dataset, what fraction did the model successfully identify? A recall of 0.9 means that out of every 10 genuine positive cases that actually existed, the model successfully caught 9 of them, missing only 1.
3. Recall Only Cares About Actual Positives

A key structural property of recall, mirroring the structural property already covered for precision but from the opposite direction, is that it entirely ignores how the model treated examples that were actually negative in the true labels. Recall is computed purely from the subset of examples that were genuinely positive, True Positives and False Negatives together, with no reference at all to True Negatives or False Positives.

This has a notable, almost mischievous edge-case consequence: a model that predicts positive for absolutely every single example in a dataset, with no discrimination whatsoever, achieves a perfect recall of 1.0, since it necessarily catches every genuine positive case by simply never once predicting negative for anything at all. Perfect recall alone, exactly as perfect precision alone did in the previous topic, says nothing at all about how many false alarms, False Positives, that same blunt, indiscriminate strategy actually generates.
4. A Concrete Illustration: Disease Screening

blocks.alt: Actually sick patients feed recall, showing how many were caught
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731756-23168765.png

Disease screening offers a clean, widely relatable illustration of what recall actually measures in practice, and it stands in useful contrast to the spam-filtering example already covered for precision. Here, predicting positive means flagging a patient for further diagnostic testing. A screening test with high recall means it successfully catches almost every patient who genuinely has the underlying disease, missing very few actual cases.

A screening test with low recall, by contrast, means many genuinely sick patients slip through undetected, incorrectly told they are healthy when they are not, a false negative with severe, potentially life-threatening real-world cost: a missed diagnosis, a disease that goes untreated and potentially worsens, precisely the kind of consequence that makes recall, not precision, the metric that matters most in a screening context like this one.
5. When False Negatives Are Especially Costly

blocks.alt: An especially costly false negative means recall should be prioritized
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731756-234339159.png

Recall becomes the single most important metric to optimize specifically in situations where a false negative carries a real, substantial cost, the direct mirror image of the situations covered for precision in the previous topic. Beyond disease screening, already covered, fraud detection offers another clear example: a false negative here means a genuinely fraudulent transaction slips through entirely unchecked, causing direct, tangible financial harm.

Security threat detection offers a third example: a false negative here means a genuine attack or intrusion goes completely unnoticed, potentially allowing serious, ongoing damage to continue unchecked simply because the detection system failed to flag it in the first place. Across every one of these situations, the shared theme mirrors precision's: whenever missing a genuine positive case causes real, substantial harm, recall becomes the metric that most directly captures the quality dimension that actually matters most.

blocks.text: 6. Recall and the Decision Threshold

blocks.alt: A lower threshold gives higher recall
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731757-111933486.png

Recall from the Precision topic's discussion of the decision threshold, defaulting to 0.5, that classifiers predicting probabilities use to convert those continuous probabilities into a final positive or negative prediction. Lowering this threshold, letting the model predict positive more readily, even without especially high confidence, directly affects recall in a predictable, opposite way from how it affected precision.

A lower threshold means the model casts a wider net, predicting positive more often overall, which tends to catch more of the genuine positive cases that actually exist, raising recall. This improvement, exactly mirroring the tradeoff covered from the opposite direction in the Precision topic, does not come free either: casting that wider net also lets more false alarms slip through as positive predictions too, meaning precision drops as a direct, unavoidable consequence of the exact same threshold adjustment.
7. Recall, Sensitivity, and True Positive Rate

It is worth being explicit about the naming variation covered briefly in this topic's overview, since encountering these different terms across different sources can otherwise cause genuine confusion. Recall, Sensitivity, and True Positive Rate all refer to the exact same underlying calculation, True Positives divided by True Positives plus False Negatives, just favored by different fields and different specific contexts.

Sensitivity is the term most commonly encountered in medical and clinical testing literature, exactly the disease-screening context already covered earlier in this topic. True Positive Rate is the specific term used inside the ROC Curve topic, covered later in this module, where it is paired directly against the False Positive Rate to build that curve's two axes. Recognizing that all three names describe the identical calculation avoids unnecessary confusion when moving between different sources, papers, or tools that each happen to favor a different one of these three names.

blocks.text: 8. A Cautionary Extreme: Recall Alone Is Not Enough

blocks.alt: Predicting everyone as positive gives perfect recall but a useless model
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731758-408439673.png

Recall has its own genuine blind spot worth understanding directly, mirroring the extreme case already covered for precision but from the opposite direction. Consider a model that simply predicts positive for every single example in an entire evaluation dataset, with absolutely no discrimination based on the actual input features at all.

This model achieves a perfect recall of 1.0, since it necessarily catches every single genuine positive case by construction, never once predicting negative for anything. Despite this seemingly flawless recall, this same model also flags every single genuinely negative example as a false positive too, an indiscriminate, essentially useless strategy in most real applications. High recall alone says absolutely nothing about how many false alarms that same blunt strategy generates, a genuinely important dimension of quality recall cannot capture on its own, and exactly the gap precision, covered in the previous topic, measures directly.
9. Precision versus Recall: The Fundamental Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Precision and recall trade off against each other
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439731759-236900125.png

With both metrics now covered in full, it is worth stating the fundamental tradeoff between them directly and clearly. Precision asks, of predicted positives, how many were correct, and is optimized by making the model more selective, predicting positive only when it is genuinely confident, exactly the higher-threshold strategy covered in the Precision topic. Recall asks, of actual positives, how many were caught, and is optimized by casting a wider net, predicting positive more readily even with less certainty, exactly the lower-threshold strategy covered earlier in this topic.

Because both metrics are tuned through the exact same underlying lever, the decision threshold, pulling one of these two metrics up by adjusting that threshold typically pulls the other one down as a direct, largely unavoidable consequence. This fundamental tension, between being selective enough to avoid false alarms and being thorough enough to avoid missing genuine cases, is precisely what F1 Score, the very next topic in this module, was built to balance directly into a single combined number.
10. Worked Example
The example below computes recall for a disease-screening classifier at two different decision thresholds, directly illustrating the precision-recall tradeoff covered in this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, precision_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X_healthy = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=2, size=(180, 2))
X_sick = rng.normal(loc=[4, 4], scale=2, size=(20, 2))
X = np.vstack([X_healthy, X_sick])
y = np.array([0] * 180 + [1] * 20)  # 1 = has the disease

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y)

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

for threshold in [0.5, 0.2]:
    predictions = (probabilities >= threshold).astype(int)
    recall = recall_score(y_test, predictions)
    precision = precision_score(y_test, predictions, zero_division=0)
    print(f"Threshold={threshold}: recall={recall:.3f} (caught this fraction of sick patients), "
          f"precision={precision:.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 typically increases recall, catching more genuinely sick patients, while precision drops, since the model now flags more healthy patients as positive too, exactly the tradeoff covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Recall measures, of every genuine positive case, what fraction the model caught: True Positives divided by all actual positives.
It ignores how the model treated actual negatives entirely, focusing purely on how thoroughly it finds genuine positives.
It matters most whenever a false negative carries a real, substantial cost: disease screening, fraud detection, security threat detection.
Lowering a classifier's decision threshold generally increases recall, at the cost of lower precision.
Recall, Sensitivity, and True Positive Rate all refer to the exact same underlying calculation, just favored by different contexts.
Perfect recall alone says nothing about how many false alarms the model generates, the mirror image of precision's blind spot.
Precision and recall are tuned through the same decision threshold, and pulling one up typically pulls the other down.
This fundamental tension is exactly what F1 Score, covered next, was built to balance into a single combined number.
Next up: F1 Score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both into one metric.
